title: Path Params, Query Params, Headers, and Bodies
summary: Read every part of a request, from path and query parameters to headers and JSON bodies, and shape the JSON you send back.
intro: A route gets a request to the right handler. Then the handler has to read it: which room, which filters, which page, who's asking, and what they sent. That information arrives in five places, each with its own rules, and almost everything a client sends arrives as plain text that your code has to turn into real values. Read it carelessly, and you get the classic API bugs: lists that skip items, a body that's silently ignored, an update that wipes a field. This lesson goes through each place in turn, the path, the query string, the headers, and the body, then ends with the other half of the job: the JSON Roombook sends back.

steps.title: Where request data lives
steps.body:
Every piece of information in a request has a place where it belongs, and putting it in the right one isn't just tidiness. Caches, logs, browsers, and proxies all treat each place differently, so the place decides who sees the data, what gets saved, and what can be bookmarked or shared.

```diagram request-data-parts
Each place has one job. Everything but the body arrives as plain text.
```

## Five places, five jobs

- **The path** says which thing: `/v1/rooms/3` is room 3. It's the resource's identity, so it's what gets bookmarked, linked, and cached.
- **The query string**, the part after `?`, holds options for reading: which rooms to include, in what order, which page. `/v1/rooms?building=main-library` is still the list of rooms, seen through a filter.
- **Headers** describe the request itself: what format the body is in, what format the client wants back, who's calling, and conditions like only if it changed.
- **The body** carries the content of a POST, PUT, or PATCH: the booking to make, the fields to change.
- **Cookies** carry the session, recall from the web course: the browser sends them back in a `Cookie` header on every request to the site. The authentication lesson builds Roombook's logins on them.

One rule follows from this: never put secrets in the URL. Paths and query strings end up in server logs, in browser history, and in the logs of every proxy along the way. Passwords, tokens, and keys go in headers, which those tools don't save by default.

## Where Express puts each one

| Place | In Express | For `/v1/rooms/3?limit=20` |
|---|---|---|
| Path parameters | `req.params` | `req.params.roomId` is `"3"` |
| Query string | `req.query` | `req.query.limit` is `"20"` |
| Headers | `req.get(name)` | `req.get("Accept")` |
| Body | `req.body` | only after a body parser ran |
| Cookies | `req.get("Cookie")` | the raw text, until the authentication lesson |

Express parses the path and the query string for you. The body needs a parser, the `express.json()` line in `app.ts`, and cookies need one too, which the authentication lesson adds.

## It's all text

Look at the values in that table: `"3"` and `"20"`, in quotes. The path, the query string, and the headers are plain text, every character of them, so Express can only hand you strings. Turning them into numbers, dates, and lists is your job, and it's where many bugs start. `"20" > "3"` is false in JavaScript, since strings compare letter by letter, and `"3" + 1` is `"31"`.

The JSON body is the one exception. JSON has its own types, numbers, true and false, null, lists, and objects, so `express.json()` gives you real values: `{"attendees": 3}` arrives as the number 3. But JSON has no type for dates, so a time like `"2026-10-05T14:00:00Z"` still arrives as a string. And the client chose every value, so a field you expect to be a number might be a string, or missing. The lesson on validation and errors checks every value at the edge, and this lesson shows where each one comes from.

The example below makes all of this visible, with a small server that answers with exactly what it received.

examples.title: A server that echoes what it got
examples.prompt: A demo, not part of Roombook: `src/echo.ts`, run with `node src/echo.ts` while the dev server is stopped. It sends back the parts of each POST it receives.
examples.explanation: `express.json()` sits in the route itself here, between the path and the handler, so only this route parses JSON bodies. In Roombook it runs once for every route, from `app.ts`. The handler copies each part of the request into the answer: the path parameters, the parsed query string, one header, and the parsed body. `req.get` looks a header up by name, and the next example asks for `content-type` in lowercase on purpose.

examples.title: Sending it every kind of data
examples.prompt: One request with a path parameter, two query parameters, one of them twice, and a JSON body. The quotes around the URL stop the terminal from reading `&` as its own symbol.
examples.explanation: `roomId` is `"3"`, a string, though it looks like a number. The query's `date` is a string too. `amenity` appeared twice, so Express made it a list of both values, which the next part relies on. `content-type` was found even though curl sent `Content-Type`, since header names ignore capital letters. In the body, `attendees` is the number 3 and `note` is a real `null`, because JSON has those types. Every value from outside the body came in as text.

steps.title: Query parameters: filters, sorting, and pages

examples.title: Filtering by building and amenity
examples.prompt: Rooms in the Main Library that have a whiteboard. The URL is in quotes because of the `&`.
examples.explanation: Hopper is in the Science Library, so the building filter dropped it. Lovelace and Turing both have a whiteboard. They come back sorted by name, the default, so Lovelace is first. Both fit on one page of 20, so `nextCursor` is `null`: there's nothing more to fetch. A client checks that one field to know whether to ask again, instead of guessing from how many items came back.

examples.title: Two pages, two rooms at a time
examples.prompt: The first command sorts by capacity with pages of 2, and `-w '\n'` ends its answer with a line break. The second sends back the `nextCursor` the first one returned.
examples.explanation: The first page holds the two smallest rooms, Lovelace with 4 and Turing with 6, and a cursor. Decoded, the cursor is `{"after":[6,1]}`: after the room with capacity 6 and id 1, which is Turing. The second page starts right after it, with Hopper, and its `nextCursor` is `null`, since that was the last room. The client never had to know what was inside the cursor, only to pass it back.

examples.title: A limit over the maximum
examples.prompt: Ask for 500 rooms in one page.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 422 Unprocessable Entity
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 67
ETag: W/"43-XaqkhJkXkiiJjV+B4FiI3hwij+k"
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:57:05 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5

{"status":422,"title":"limit must be a whole number from 1 to 100"}
examples.explanation: The request was fine to read, a query string with a number in it, but the number broke Roombook's rule, so the answer is a 422 whose title says what's allowed. Node.js prints the code's older name, Unprocessable Entity, and the number is what counts. Quietly using 100 instead would have been the other choice, and it hides the client's mistake: they'd think they got everything. An error says it plainly.

steps.title: Headers: about the request and the answer
steps.body:
Headers are where a request and a response describe themselves: what format they're in, who's asking, and under what conditions. They're easy to overlook, since curl hides them unless you ask, and they're behind some of an API's most useful tricks, like answering a repeated read with no body at all.

## Request headers Roombook reads

| Header | What it says | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `Content-Type` | the format of the body | `application/json` |
| `Accept` | the formats the client can read | `application/json` |
| `Authorization` | the caller's credentials | `Bearer eyJhbGciOi...` |
| `If-None-Match` | send it only if it changed | `W/"63-NSrfY7GWv7SI..."` |
| `If-Match` | change it only if it hasn't changed | `"3"` |
| `Idempotency-Key` | a retry of an earlier request | `9f1c2e7a-...` |

The authentication lesson reads `Authorization`, the lesson on constraints and transactions uses `If-Match`, and the lesson on retries and idempotency uses `Idempotency-Key`. In Express, `req.get("Idempotency-Key")` returns a header's value, or `undefined` when it's missing.

## Response headers Roombook sends

| Header | What it says |
|---|---|
| `Location` | where the new or moved resource is |
| `Cache-Control` | who may keep a copy of the answer, and for how long |
| `ETag` | a fingerprint of this version of the resource |
| `Retry-After` | how long to wait before trying again, after a 429 or 503 |

`Cache-Control` suits data that rarely changes. Roombook's buildings change about once a year, so the list says any cache may keep it for five minutes:

```ts
buildingRoutes.get("/", (_req, res) => {
  res.set("Cache-Control", "public, max-age=300");
  res.json({ items: buildings, nextCursor: null });
});
```

`public` means any cache along the way may store it, and `max-age=300` means for 300 seconds. Answers that depend on who's asking, like a user's own bookings, must never be `public`, or a shared cache could hand one person's bookings to another. For those, use `private` or `no-store`, which the Redis lesson comes back to.

## Two rules for names

Header names ignore capital letters: `Content-Type`, `content-type`, and `CONTENT-TYPE` are the same header. Node.js turns every name to lowercase in `req.headers`, and `req.get` accepts any spelling. HTTP/2, recall from the web course, even sends them all in lowercase.

A header you invent needs no `X-` at the start. That prefix was once the custom for headers outside the standards, but headers that started as `X-` and later became standard had to keep the awkward name forever, so the custom was dropped in 2012. That's why it's `Idempotency-Key`, not `X-Idempotency-Key`. You'll still meet old ones like `X-Request-Id`, which the next lesson uses because everyone already does.

## ETag and 304: nothing new to send

Every JSON answer from Express has had an `ETag` header, a fingerprint of the body that Express computes by itself. A client that saved the room, and its `ETag`, can later ask for it again with `If-None-Match` and the fingerprint. If the room is unchanged, the fingerprint matches, and Express answers **304 Not Modified** with no body: your copy is still good. If it changed, the client gets a normal 200 with the new room and a new `ETag`.

That saves the bandwidth of the body, which matters on a phone, and browsers do it on their own for anything they've cached. It doesn't save the server's work, since Express built the whole answer to fingerprint it. The `W/` in front marks a **weak** ETag, one that promises the same meaning without promising the exact same bytes. The lesson on constraints and transactions gives each room a version number, which makes an ETag Roombook can check without building the body, and lets `If-Match` stop two people's edits from overwriting each other.

examples.title: Asking again with If-None-Match
examples.prompt: The first command reads room 1 and shows its `ETag`, with `-w '\n'` to end the answer with a line break. The second sends that `ETag` back.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 99
ETag: W/"63-NSrfY7GWv7SId8XCn7/vZtgopSo"
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:57:05 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5

{"id":1,"name":"Turing","building":"main-library","capacity":6,"amenities":["whiteboard","screen"]}
HTTP/1.1 304 Not Modified
ETag: W/"63-NSrfY7GWv7SId8XCn7/vZtgopSo"
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:57:05 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5
examples.explanation: The first answer is a full 200 with the room, 99 bytes. The second is a 304 with the same `ETag` and no body, since the room hadn't changed. Express compared the fingerprints for you, in `res.json`, before sending anything. The `63` at the start of the fingerprint is the body's length in hexadecimal, 99, and the rest is a hash of the body. Change the room with a PATCH, and the same second command gets a 200 again, with the new room and a new fingerprint.

examples.title: The buildings list, with Cache-Control
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Cache-Control: public, max-age=300
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 275
ETag: W/"113-g00xelp0aKtlmG+w1JQU2ng02JY"
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:57:05 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5

{"items":[{"id":1,"slug":"main-library","name":"Main Library","timezone":"America/New_York","opensAt":"08:00","closesAt":"22:00"},{"id":2,"slug":"science-library","name":"Science Library","timezone":"America/New_York","opensAt":"09:00","closesAt":"18:00"}],"nextCursor":null}
examples.explanation: `Cache-Control` came first, since the handler set it before `res.json` added the rest. A browser that calls this from a web page keeps the answer for five minutes, and repeats within that time never reach Roombook at all. After that, it asks again with `If-None-Match`, and gets a 304 while the list is unchanged. Each building has its slug, the name the rooms filter uses, and its opening hours, written as local times in the building's time zone, `America/New_York`, which later lessons need to check that a booking falls inside them.

steps.title: The request body

examples.title: A form post instead of JSON
examples.prompt: `-d` on its own sends the body as form data, the way an HTML form would.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 415 Unsupported Media Type
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 42
ETag: W/"2a-oGlpVD6dWcEgbmcqMmcg365L2kQ"
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:57:05 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5

{"status":415,"title":"Body must be JSON"}
examples.explanation: curl sent `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded`. `express.json()` skipped the body, `requireJson` saw a type that isn't JSON, and the request never reached the handler that creates rooms. The 415 and its title tell the client's developer exactly what to fix: send JSON. Without `requireJson`, the handler would have read `name` from an undefined body, crashed, and answered 500.

examples.title: Too big, and broken
examples.prompt: `big.json` is a 200 KB booking with a very long note, saved in the folder you run curl from. The second body is JSON cut off halfway. `-w '%{http_code}'` prints only the status code.
examples.explanation: The `@` in `--json @big.json` tells curl to send the file's contents. Express stopped reading at 100 KB and answered 413, and the handler never saw the request. The broken body got a 400, since it couldn't be parsed at all. That's the 400 and 422 split from the routes lesson: 400 when the request can't be read, 422 when it can, and a value breaks a rule.

examples.title: Keeping a note, then clearing it
examples.prompt: Booking 1002 has the note Chemistry revision. The first patch leaves the note out, and the second sets it to null. `-w '\n'` keeps the two answers on separate lines.
examples.code:
curl -w '\n' -X PATCH --json '{"attendees": 4}' http://localhost:4000/v1/bookings/1002
curl -X PATCH --json '{"note": null}' http://localhost:4000/v1/bookings/1002
examples.explanation: After the first patch, `attendees` is 4 and the note is untouched, since `Object.hasOwn` found no `note` field. After the second, the note is `null`, since the field was there with `null` as its value. `version` went up with each change, which the repository's `update` does every time. Booking 1002 comes from the next part's first example, so create it first if your server restarted.

steps.title: Responses and the handler's job
steps.body:
A handler's last step, the response, is the contract clients code against. Every field name, every time format, and every null is something a web app or a phone app will depend on, and changing it later breaks them. So Roombook decides these once, and every handler follows the same rules.

## Parse, check, act, respond

Every handler does the same four things, in this order:

1. **Parse**: turn the request's text into values, like an id from the path or a `RoomQuery` from the query string.
2. **Check**: refuse what's wrong, with the right code, before changing anything. Is the id valid, is the room there, are the values allowed.
3. **Act**: do the work, usually through the repository.
4. **Respond**: turn the result into JSON, with the right status and headers.

Keeping that order means a request that fails a check never changes anything, so an error never leaves half a booking behind. The lesson on validation and errors moves the parse and check steps into schemas, and the lesson on services and repositories moves the act step into a service, but the order stays.

## Roombook's JSON rules

- **Field names are camelCase**, like `startsAt` and `roomId`: the style of JavaScript itself, and of most JSON APIs.
- **Times are strings in RFC 3339 format, in UTC, to the second**, like `"2026-10-05T14:00:00Z"`. RFC 3339 is the standard way to write a date and time, and the `Z` at the end means UTC, the time zone with no offset. One zone for every time means a client never has to guess.
- **Ids are whole numbers**, like `1002`. A JavaScript number holds whole numbers exactly up to about 9 quadrillion, which Roombook won't reach.
- **Every field is always there.** A note that's empty is `"note": null`, never a missing field. A client can rely on the shape without checking first whether a field exists.
- **Lists are objects**: `{"items": [...], "nextCursor": ...}`, even when there's only one page.

## Never send what you store

From this lesson on, Roombook's bookings repository stores times as `Date` objects, the way the raw SQL lesson's database driver will hand them back. The stored record also has fields that aren't part of the contract, like `cancelledAt`, the moment a booking was cancelled, which Roombook keeps for its own records. So no handler sends a stored booking as it is. Each one passes through a **view**, a function that builds exactly the JSON the contract promises, in `src/modules/bookings/bookings.view.ts`:

```ts
export function toBookingView(booking: Booking) {
  return {
    id: booking.id,
    roomId: booking.roomId,
    userId: booking.userId,
    startsAt: toUtcString(booking.startsAt),
    endsAt: toUtcString(booking.endsAt),
    attendees: booking.attendees,
    note: booking.note,
    status: booking.status,
    version: booking.version,
    createdAt: toUtcString(booking.createdAt),
  };
}
```

`toUtcString`, in `src/http/time.ts`, writes a `Date` the way the contract says. JavaScript's own `toISOString` adds milliseconds, like `14:00:00.000Z`, which is valid RFC 3339 but isn't Roombook's format, so it trims them:

```ts
export function toUtcString(date: Date): string {
  return date.toISOString().replace(/\.\d{3}Z$/, "Z");
}
```

Every handler that answers with a booking calls it: `res.json(toBookingView(booking))`. It lists each field by name, so `cancelledAt` stays inside, and a new field added to storage later, like a user's password hash in the authentication lesson, can never leak into a response by accident. It's also where the format rules live, in one place: every time goes through `toUtcString`. And it lets storage change without changing the API, which is what the raw SQL lesson will need when the records come from a database.

## Accept and 406

A client says which formats it can read in the `Accept` header. Roombook only speaks JSON, so a client that accepts only, say, `text/csv` can't be served, and the honest answer is **406 Not Acceptable**. In Express, `req.accepts("json")` returns false for that client. Most clients send `Accept: application/json` or `*/*`, which means anything, so Roombook can leave this check out until it ever offers a second format.

The next lesson covers middleware, the code that runs around every handler, like the `requireJson` check from part 4.

examples.title: A booking made in another time zone
examples.prompt: A student's phone set to UTC+2 sends local times, written with a `+02:00` offset.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: /v1/bookings/1002
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
Content-Length: 209
ETag: W/"d1-vg6pl/gOPjT1aCiBQaJM4Z3Ib90"
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 23:57:05 GMT
Connection: keep-alive
Keep-Alive: timeout=5

{"id":1002,"roomId":2,"userId":1,"startsAt":"2026-10-05T14:00:00Z","endsAt":"2026-10-05T15:00:00Z","attendees":2,"note":"Chemistry revision","status":"confirmed","version":1,"createdAt":"2026-10-01T09:00:00Z"}
examples.explanation: The handler parsed each time with `new Date(...)`, which understands the offset, and the view wrote it back in UTC: 16:00 at UTC+2 is 14:00 UTC. The client sent one format, and every client reads the same format back. `createdAt` is Roombook's story clock, 1 October 2026 at 9:00 UTC, which stands in for the real time. The lesson on services and repositories shows how the code reads it, from a clock passed in like any other dependency. The stored booking also has `cancelledAt`, set to `null`, and the view left it out.

examples.title: Reading a booking through its view
examples.prompt: The seeded booking, Ada's study group in Turing.
examples.explanation: Every field the contract promises is there, in the order the view lists them, in camelCase, with every time in UTC. Monday 5 October from 14:00 to 15:30 UTC is a 90-minute booking, on the 30-minute boundaries Roombook's rules require. The same view serves the GET, the POST, the PATCH, and the cancel action, so all four answers have the same shape, and a client needs only one type for a booking.

recap:
- The path names the thing, the query string holds options, headers describe the request, the body carries content, and cookies carry the session.
- Path, query, and headers arrive as text, so turn them into real values yourself, and never put secrets in a URL.
- Express 5's query parser makes repeated names into arrays, and req.query is read-only, so parse it into a new object.
- Give list parameters defaults and bounds, sort from an allowlist, and page with an opaque cursor, not an offset.
- Header names ignore case, new ones need no X- prefix, and an ETag with If-None-Match gives a 304 with no body.
- Accept only JSON bodies, with 415 for other types, 413 over the size limit, and 400 for broken JSON.
- Tell a missing field from a null one with Object.hasOwn, so a PATCH can clear a value.
- Send camelCase JSON with UTC times to the second and every field present, built by a view, never the stored record.
